source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
Per CoreSite's own facility page, this building, VA3, is located at 12369 Sunrise Valley Drive, Reston, VA 20191, part of CoreSite's three-building Reston campus alongside VA1 and VA2. CoreSite publishes 533,000-plus square feet for VA3 on the main facility page. The operator's spec-sheet landing page separately cites "more than 940,000 square feet," a figure that reads as a campus-wide aggregate given its accompanying framing, "Since 2007, CoreSite has been delivering operational excellence in the NoVa market," rather than a VA3-specific number, so this entry uses the building-specific 533,000-plus figure instead. No MW capacity or opening year is stated. The operator does cite N+2 generator redundancy and participation in the NVIDIA DGX-Ready Data Center program. CoreSite lists SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and HIPAA compliance generally across its portfolio, without breaking those certifications out by building.

Virginia's data center boom is reshaping statewide electricity rates directly relevant to this Reston campus. In November 2026, the Virginia State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates raising a typical residential bill by about $16 a month to roughly $165, while creating a new GS-5 rate class for data centers effective January 1, 2027, under which facilities with 25 megawatts or more of demand face 14-year mandatory contracts and minimum cost-coverage requirements, per Inside Climate News. American Tower, CoreSite's parent, reported record leasing at CoreSite driving stronger-than-expected second-quarter 2026 results, projecting data-center segment revenue of $1.20 billion to $1.22 billion for full-year 2026, roughly 14.9 percent growth at the midpoint, and raised its full-year outlook on the strength of that performance. The company also budgeted approximately $695 million in data-center development spending for 2026. As CoreSite's largest published Reston building, VA3's NVIDIA DGX-Ready designation reflects a broader industry push among colocation operators to certify AI-workload readiness alongside traditional enterprise colocation offerings. VA3 is a physically separate building from VA1 and VA2 on the same Reston campus, and CoreSite's public materials do not attribute a campus-wide power figure the way some Loudoun County operators do, leaving prospective tenants to confirm available capacity directly with CoreSite rather than from any published aggregate.

profile.campus_power_note: CoreSite does not publish a campus-wide MW figure for its three-building Reston campus (VA1, VA2, VA3). Only building-level square footage is published, and only for some buildings. VA3's own facility page confirms 533,000-plus sq ft for this building specifically.

reading.body:
CoreSite VA3 publishes 533,000 square feet of technical space but no IT load figure in megawatts, making it impossible to assess its role in AI infrastructure scaling based on disclosed capacity.

Without a published power number, the facility's actual compute density remains opaque. A 533,000-square-foot campus almost certainly houses substantial power capacity, but size alone cannot be translated into rack counts or accelerator counts without operator disclosure. This gap matters because AI workloads are power-constrained, not space-constrained. A facility can be physically large and still underpowered relative to modern accelerator demand, or fully utilized at lower densities for non-AI workloads.

The six certifications, SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and HIPAA, qualify VA3 for regulated inference and data processing rather than frontier training. These certifications indicate the campus is built for workloads requiring financial audit trails, information security governance, federal compliance, payment card handling, or health data protection. None are specific to AI training density. They open doors to AI-adjacent work, but do not indicate whether the facility prioritizes the high-voltage, high-cooling infrastructure that training at scale requires.

Virginia hosts 326 mapped data center facilities and 1,326 MW of published capacity across just 19 that disclosed a power figure. VA3 ranks outside those 19, meaning CoreSite has chosen not to publish the megawatt specification that would place it in the competitive ranking. In the most densely developed data center market in the United States, non-disclosure of power capacity is itself a data point. It signals that either the facility serves use cases where raw power numbers do not drive buyer decisions, or that the operator prefers opacity in a state where capacity numbers are otherwise public.
